To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) children with a history of severe malnutrition have a higher risk of developing obesity and diabetes in adulthood, and that 2) a low protein intake in childhood and adolescence increases the risk of developing obesity in adulthood.
the intake of dietary protein and energy in adult survivors of severe malnutrition depends on the type of malnutrition and the amount of energy and protein provided in the rehabilitation diet.
a high PEP diet is associated with increased weight gain and increased risk of becoming overweight or obese in adulthood.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how the early life environment, particularly the maternal and infant diet, can influence the risk of later obesity, and the mechanisms by which these effects may be mediated.
how the early life environment influences later life health, and in particular how early life nutrition and stress influence the regulation of energy homeostasis.
the effects of protein on energy metabolism, appetite and body composition.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

protein is essential for the development of lean body mass, but the exact role of protein and amino acids in the control of appetite, body fat mass, body fat distribution and body composition is not yet fully understood.
the relationship between birthweight and macronutrient intake is not linear.
a diet high in protein is not only safe, but also healthy and beneficial to the body.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we found that the effects of protein on appetite and satiety are dependent on the macronutrient content of the diet.
there is no evidence for an effect of early life nutrition on macronutrient preference in adulthood.
the developmental origins of health and disease are not limited to the prenatal and neonatal periods, but that the effects of early malnutrition may be expressed in later life.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the macronutrient composition of the food we eat matters.
the protein intake of children and adolescents is not adequate, even in countries with high per capita income.

we should be more careful about the way we use the term ‘nutrient’ in the context of food choice, as the way that we define nutrients may not reflect the way people perceive them, and this may have important consequences for the way that we develop and evaluate interventions aimed at promoting healthy eating.
